name: Temporal
summary: A durable workflow platform that separates request admission, workflow-history ownership, task matching, and application workers so workflow progress can be reconstructed from recorded events while external work is retried at explicit boundaries.
scope: Frontend, History, Matching, and internal Worker services
task queues, timers, and workflow messages
deterministic replay, versioning, activities, and retries

features.name: Independently scalable service roles
features.description: The Temporal Server separates a stateless Frontend gateway for validation, authorization, rate limiting, and routing from History for workflow state, Matching for user-facing task queues, and an internal Worker Service for system workflows. History, Matching, and Worker services can scale horizontally, while Frontend has no service sharding.
benefits: Allows scaling and troubleshooting to follow different service workloads
Makes the request, durable-state, dispatch, and internal-maintenance boundaries explicit
costs: Adds service-to-service coordination and membership discovery
Independent deployment increases operational topology and failure modes

features.name: Namespace configuration and access boundary
features.description: Current official documentation defines a Namespace as the scope for Workflow Executions and Task Queues, Workflow ID uniqueness, and settings such as retention and archival. In the pinned source, namespace configuration and Frontend authorization are concrete code paths; self-hosted transport security remains a separate TLS/mTLS configuration. The current documentation's resource-isolation and Nexus guarantees are recorded as documentation-date context, not silently applied to the pinned revision.
benefits: Separates identity/configuration domains while retaining one service cluster
Makes cross-namespace communication an explicit interface
costs: A shared Namespace remains multi-tenant and requires naming coordination
Isolation and security properties depend on deployment configuration and authorization plugins

features.name: History-shard-owned workflow persistence
features.description: A History Shard maps to a persistence partition and owns Workflow Execution Event History, mutable state, and internal transfer, timer, replication, and visibility task queues. Workflow metadata such as Namespace and Workflow ID is hashed to choose a shard; shard ownership uses a range ID to serialize and reject stale writes in the inspected source.
benefits: Provides a concrete serialization and placement unit for workflow state
Makes durable timers and internal follow-up work part of the history ownership boundary
costs: The configured shard count is a long-lived capacity decision
Shard-local serialization and per-shard overhead constrain placement and throughput

features.name: Queue-mediated task dispatch
features.description: History emits workflow progress and tasks to the Matching subsystem, which hosts user-facing Task Queues and matches tasks to polling Workers. Task queues belong to a Namespace and route work to compatible worker pools; queue backlog and worker availability therefore mediate progress without becoming workflow-local state.
benefits: Decouples durable orchestration from application worker capacity
Supports routing and independent worker pools for workflow and activity execution
costs: Scheduling latency and backlog affect progress
Queue and worker configuration become part of the operational contract

features.name: Event-history replay for state recovery
features.description: A Worker re-executes deterministic Workflow code and compares generated Commands with the existing Event History. Recorded events reconstruct workflow-local state after worker or service interruption; a Worker cache and sticky queue can avoid replay until eviction, but cached state is an optimization rather than the durable record.
benefits: Recovers workflow-local state without serializing arbitrary in-memory state
Makes failure recovery inspectable through the event sequence
costs: Replay consumes worker CPU and long histories increase recovery work
A command mismatch can produce a nondeterminism failure

features.name: Durable timers and typed workflow messages
features.description: Workflow APIs turn timers and external interaction into recorded workflow progress. Queries read state without adding history events, Signals are asynchronous writes recorded in history, and Updates are validated and tracked synchronous writes whose acceptance and completion are recorded. Message payloads and results must be serializable.
benefits: Provides explicit read, asynchronous-write, and synchronous-write interfaces to a stateful workflow
Makes timer and message outcomes replayable and observable
costs: Query responsiveness depends on an available polling Worker
Signals and Updates require handler lifecycle and concurrency discipline; un-drained messages can be lost at completion or Continue-As-New

features.name: Activity failure and retry boundary
features.description: External or nondeterministic work belongs in Activities outside the replay path. Activity attempts are governed by timeout and retry policy and their results or failures are represented in workflow history; retries can repeat external effects, so idempotency or compensation remains an application responsibility.
benefits: Separates deterministic orchestration from unreliable side effects
Makes transient failure handling explicit at the activity boundary
costs: Retries increase load and latency and may duplicate effects
Timeout and retry policy do not make an external system transactional

features.name: History-backed workflow versioning
features.description: Long-running workflows must preserve deterministic replay across code changes. Worker Versioning and history-recorded patching with GetVersion allow new executions to take new paths while existing executions retain compatible behavior; old branches can be removed only after relevant executions leave retention.
benefits: Makes rolling evolution of long-lived state an explicit design concern
Preserves replay compatibility without freezing all workflow code
costs: Version branches accumulate and require lifecycle tracking
Removing a branch too early can make old histories unreplayable

mathematical_views.question: How do commands, events, timers, messages, and activity results define the reachable states of one Workflow Execution while Namespace and Workflow ID determine identity and admission?
assumptions: The event history is the durable execution record for the modeled execution
Workflow code is deterministic for the history being replayed
Namespace access control and resource isolation are modeled as configured boundaries, not unconditional properties of every deployment
The view omits database-specific transaction implementation

mathematical_views.question: How does hashing workflow identity to a History Shard, then guarding persistence writes with shard ownership, distribute workflow state while preserving a per-shard serialization boundary?
assumptions: A History Shard corresponds to one persistence partition as documented
The inspected source's range-ID ownership checks represent the relevant stale-writer guard
The model does not claim global ordering across shards

mathematical_views.question: How do Frontend admission, History task creation, Matching queue selection, and Worker polling form a distributed path whose scheduling delay is separate from workflow state?
assumptions: Task queues route only to compatible polling workers
Queue backlog and worker availability are environmental variables
The view does not imply exactly-once task delivery or end-to-end transactionality

mathematical_views.question: Which observations are preserved when deterministic workflow replay reconstructs local state while Activities perform external effects and return recorded results?
assumptions: Commands are compared against the existing history during replay
Activity effects are idempotent, compensated, or otherwise safe under configured retries
The model explicitly excludes a claim that replay or retries provide an external transaction

mathematical_views.question: Under what relation between old workflow code, version markers, worker deployments, and retained event histories can a new implementation refine an existing execution without changing its command sequence?
assumptions: Version markers or worker routing select a replay-compatible branch
Retention has not removed histories needed by still-running executions
This is a candidate refinement view, not a proof of compatibility for arbitrary code changes

costs: More distributed coordination and operational components

benefits: Explicit identity, configuration, and access domains
costs: Security requires deployment configuration; shared namespaces need coordination

benefits: Durable state and serialized ownership unit
costs: Shard sizing is a durable capacity decision

benefits: Independent worker scaling and routing
costs: Backlog and worker availability affect latency

benefits: Recoverable local state and inspectable progress
costs: Replay cost and nondeterminism sensitivity

benefits: Typed stateful workflow interfaces
costs: Handler availability and lifecycle constraints

benefits: Structured recovery around external work
costs: Repeated effects and retry load

benefits: Evolution of long-lived executions
costs: Version branch and retention management
